_help: The source types shown in the APA Reference Guide. See README.md, 'How to add or edit a source type'. *text* = italics. {A} = author part, {D} = date part. Patterns and examples follow the UTS APA 7th referencing guide (January 2025) unless the 'ref' field says otherwise. All example authors and titles are invented. 'case' lists the parts of each reference and whether they use sentence case, title case or the name as written (shown in the Capital letters note).

groups.title: Most used
groups.about: The sources most students cite in essays and reports.

sources.title: Journal article
sources.when: An article from an academic journal, found online or in a library database.
sources.pattern: {A} ({D}). Article title. *Journal Title*, *volume*(issue), page range. https://doi.org/xxxx
sources.example: {A} ({D}). Short study sessions and long-term memory. *Journal of Student Learning*, *14*(2), 45-58. https://doi.org/10.1234/jsl.2021.0142

none.pattern: Article title. ({D}). *Journal Title*, *volume*(issue), page range. https://doi.org/xxxx
none.example: Short study sessions and long-term memory. ({D}). *Journal of Student Learning*, *14*(2), 45-58. https://doi.org/10.1234/jsl.2021.0142

tips: The journal title and the volume number are in italics. The issue number is not.
Only the first word of the article title (and the first word after a colon) has a capital letter.
No DOI? Leave it out.
No issue number? Leave out the brackets and the issue number.
Online-only articles may have an article number instead of pages: …, *14*, Article e0142. https://doi.org/…

case.example: Short study sessions and long-term memory

sources.title: Book
sources.when: A whole book written by the same author(s) throughout.
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *Writing at university: A practical guide* (2nd ed.). Harbour Press.
sources.orgExample: {A} ({D}). *Writing at university: A practical guide* (2nd ed.).

none.example: *Writing at university: A practical guide* (2nd ed.). ({D}). Harbour Press.

tips: The book title is in italics. Only the first word (and the first word after a colon) has a capital letter.
First edition? Leave out the edition: *Writing at university*. Harbour Press.
When the organisation is also the publisher, do not write its name twice: leave out the publisher.
Two publishers? Separate them with a semicolon (;).
If the book has a DOI, you can add it at the end.

sources.title: Chapter in an edited book
sources.when: A book where each chapter has different authors and the book has an editor. Cite the chapter you used.
sources.pattern: {A} ({D}). Chapter title. In A. Editor (Ed.), *Title of book* (pp. xx-xx). Publisher.
sources.example: {A} ({D}). Reading strategies for second-language students. In M. Castillo (Ed.), *Succeeding at university* (pp. 45-62). Harbour Press.
tips: The chapter authors go first. The editor goes after “In”, with the initials before the surname.
Two editors: In M. Castillo & J. Kaur (Eds.), …
Add the edition if it is not the first: *Succeeding at university* (2nd ed., pp. 45-62).
The in-text citation uses the chapter authors, not the editor.

sources.title: Web page
sources.when: A page on a website (not a news article, journal article or report).
sources.pattern: {A} ({D}). *Title of web page*. Website Name. URL
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *How to plan an essay*. Student Life Hub. https://www.example.com/essay-planning

none.pattern: *Title of web page*. ({D}). Website Name. URL
none.example: *How to plan an essay*. ({D}). Student Life Hub. https://www.example.com/essay-planning

tips: Most web pages are written by an organisation. Check the bottom of the page or the “About us” page.
When the organisation and the website have the same name, write the name only once (as the author).
Use the date the page was published or last updated. Do not use the copyright year at the bottom of the screen.
No date on the page? Choose “No date” above: the date becomes n.d.
Quoting a long page with no page numbers? Give the section or paragraph: (Rahman, 2024, Planning section) or (Rahman, 2024, para. 3).

sources.title: Online newspaper article
sources.when: A news story from a newspaper's website.
sources.example: {A} ({D}). City councils plan more bike lanes near campuses. *The Daily Courier*. https://www.example.com/news/bike-lanes

none.example: City councils plan more bike lanes near campuses. ({D}). *The Daily Courier*. https://www.example.com/news/bike-lanes

tips: The newspaper name is in italics. The article title is not.
Give the full date: year, month and day.
No author? The article title moves to the front. In the in-text citation, put the title in quotation marks with capital letters for the main words.
Print newspaper? Leave out the URL and add the page: … *The Daily Courier*, A8.

case.example: City councils plan more bike lanes near campuses

sources.title: Report (government or organisation)
sources.when: A report published by a government department, agency or organisation.
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *Bus use in growing cities*. National Centre for Urban Transport. https://www.example.org/reports/bus-use
sources.orgExample: {A} ({D}). *Bus use in growing cities* (Report No. 7). https://www.example.org/reports/bus-use
tips: The report title is in italics.
If the report has a number, put it in brackets after the title, not in italics. If it has no number, leave this out.
When people wrote the report for an organisation, the people are the authors and the organisation comes after the title.
Long organisation names can be shortened in-text after the first time (see the in-text citations below).

sources.title: Edited book (the whole book)
sources.when: You refer to a whole edited book, not one chapter. (Usually you should cite the chapter instead.)
tips: Write (Ed.) for one editor and (Eds.) for two or more.
If you used one chapter, cite the chapter instead (see “Chapter in an edited book”).

sources.title: E-book (online book)
sources.when: A book you read online with a DOI or a web address.
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *Thinking critically about sources*. Harbour Press. https://doi.org/10.1234/tcs.2020
tips: Found the e-book in a library database? Reference it like a print book (no URL).
No DOI but available on the web? Use the URL instead.
No page numbers? In a quotation, give the chapter or section and the paragraph: (Rahman, 2020, Chapter 3, para. 4).

sources.title: Online magazine article (e.g. The Conversation)
sources.when: An article from a magazine or news-and-analysis website.
sources.example: {A} ({D}). Why students should sleep before exams. *Campus Weekly*. https://www.example.com/sleep-exams
tips: The magazine name is in italics. The article title is not.
Quoting an article with no page numbers? Give the paragraph: (Rahman, 2023, para. 5).

case.example: Why students should sleep before exams

sources.title: YouTube video
sources.when: A video on YouTube (or a similar video site).
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *How to paraphrase without plagiarising* [Video]. YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=example
tips: The person or channel that uploaded the video is the author.
If you know the person's real name, write it and add the username in square brackets. If not, use the channel name only (choose “A channel or organisation” above).
Quoting the video? Give the time instead of a page: (Rahman, 2023, 1:30).

sources.title: TED talk
sources.when: A TED talk watched on ted.com (speaker as author) or on YouTube (TED as author).
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *Why small habits change cities* [Video]. TED Conferences. https://www.ted.com/talks/example
sources.orgPattern: {A} ({D}). *Speaker Name: Title of talk* [Video]. YouTube. URL
sources.orgExample: {A} ({D}). *Kwame Mensah: Why small habits change cities* [Video]. YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=example
tips: On ted.com, the speaker is the author. On YouTube, the TED channel is the author and the speaker's name goes in the title.
Quoting the talk? Give the time: (Mensah, 2022, 1:40).

sources.title: Lecture slides (online)
sources.when: Slides or handouts from your course that are online (for example on Canvas or Moodle).
sources.pattern: {A} ({D}). *Unit code Unit name, lecture or week: Title* [PowerPoint slides]. Learning platform. URL
sources.example: {A} ({D}). *ACAD101 Academic skills, week 4: Using sources* [PowerPoint slides]. Harbour University Canvas. https://canvas.example.edu/courses/101
tips: Check with your lecturer first: some courses do not want lecture slides in the reference list. Use the original sources the slides mention where you can.
Notes or handouts that are not online are cited as a personal communication (see that source type).
sources.ref: University of Sydney Library APA 7th guide, University study materials

sources.title: Generative AI (ChatGPT, Copilot, etc.)
sources.when: Text or images made by a generative AI tool. Check first that your course allows it.

authorLabels.org: The company that makes the tool

tips: Check with your tutor first. Using AI without permission may be academic misconduct.
The company is the author. The tool's name is the title.
Your course may ask you to put your prompts and the AI's answers in an appendix.
This example is the one in the UTS guide.

sources.title: Online dictionary entry
sources.when: A definition from an online dictionary or encyclopedia that is updated over time.
sources.pattern: {A} ({D}). Entry word. In *Name of dictionary*. Retrieved Month Day, Year, from URL
sources.example: {A} ({D}). Hypothesis. In *Academic Words Online dictionary*. Retrieved March 14, 2025, from https://www.example.com/hypothesis
tips: Online dictionaries change, so add the date you looked at the page (“Retrieved …”).
Most online dictionary entries have no date: n.d.

sources.title: Wikipedia page
sources.when: Many lecturers do not accept Wikipedia. Use it to find better sources, and cite those instead.
tips: Check that your course accepts Wikipedia before you use it.
Use the link to the version you read (“View history”), because Wikipedia pages change.

sources.title: Personal communication (email, conversation, class notes)
sources.when: Something a person told you privately (email, conversation, message) or notes that are not online.

inText.pattern: A. Author (personal communication, Month Day, Year)

tips: Personal communications are NOT in the reference list. You only cite them in your text.
Write the initials before the surname, and give the full date.

layout: Start the reference list on a new page, with the heading “References” in bold and centred.
Put the references in alphabetical order by the first author's surname (or by the title if there is no author).
Use a hanging indent of 1.27 cm: the first line starts at the margin and the other lines are indented. In Word: select the list, then Ctrl + T (Windows) or Cmd + T (Mac).
Book, article and web page titles: only the first word, the first word after a colon and names have capital letters (“sentence case”).
Journal, newspaper and magazine names: capitals for the main words (“title case”), in italics.
Every in-text citation needs a reference list entry (except personal communications), and every entry needs at least one in-text citation.
Used “as cited in”? Only the source you actually read goes in the reference list.
